title: The Stoic morning
hook: preview, one principle, and a clear intention

segments.voice: Yesterday: a Stoic birthday, and Seneca's honest count. Your line was how much did I live. Was there one fully lived hour? Day six hundred seventy-five.

The alarm goes off. Before your feet touch the floor, your hand has found the phone. Messages, headlines, someone's vacation, a work email marked urgent. Within ninety seconds, the day has been decided for you by whoever got there first. The turning year is behind us now. For the next stretch of the porch, we're putting a year of Stoic reading to work in ordinary life: morning, evening, work, home, the hard days and the good ones. And it starts where every day starts. Today: the Stoic morning.
screen: `THE ALARM, THE PHONE, THE HEADLINES.` → `DECIDED BY WHOEVER GOT THERE FIRST.` → `LIVING THE PORCH BEGINS.`

segments.voice: Three parts, gathered from a year of reading, mostly from Marcus. First, preview. Marcus opens book two of his notebook with this, in George Long's 1862 translation: "Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busy-body, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial." It sounds grim. But read on, and he says none of them can really harm him, and that they're his kin, made for working together. The preview isn't pessimism. It's packing an umbrella: when the rude email comes, you've already met it once, calmly, in your head. Second, one principle. Marcus tells himself to keep his principles ready the way a doctor keeps instruments close at hand for sudden cases. Not a whole philosophy. One line for the day. Maybe Epictetus's split: some things are up to me, some aren't. Maybe Seneca's: begin now. Maybe one you've written yourself this year. Third, intention. On the mornings Marcus didn't want to get up, and he admits there were many, he asks himself what he was made for: to lie under the blankets keeping warm, or to do the work of a human being? An intention answers that for today. Not a to-do list. A how: patient with my kids, honest in the meeting, kind on the phone. Fourth, the whole thing takes about two minutes. Preview, principle, intention. Before the phone, if you can. The day will still surprise you. But you'll meet it as yourself, rather than as whoever the first notification decided you'd be.
screen: `PREVIEW: MEET THE DAY ONCE, CALMLY.` · `ONE PRINCIPLE, READY AT HAND.` · `INTENTION: THE WORK OF A HUMAN BEING.` · `TWO MINUTES, BEFORE THE PHONE.` · then, large: `PREVIEW, PRINCIPLE, INTENTION.`

segments.voice: Let's do a Stoic morning now, whatever time it is. Preview: picture the rest of your day. Where's the likely friction, a person, a task, a delay? Meet it once in your mind, calmly. Principle: choose one line to carry, from this year or your own. Say it silently. Intention: finish this sentence for yourself, today I want to be someone who. Then sit with all three, and let them settle. The bell holds the time.
The Stoic morning: a two-minute start, preview the day, choose one principle, set a clear intention, before the world decides for you. Today's word.
Your line: preview, principle, intention. Tomorrow morning, before you touch your phone, give those three their two minutes. Day six hundred seventy-five.

howItsDone: Many modern Stoic practitioners begin the day with a short routine drawn from Marcus and Epictetus: previewing difficulties, recalling one principle, and setting an intention.

original.note: Latin: the rehearsal of hardships ahead, a later name for the Stoic preview.

trapdoor: what you thought: a Stoic morning means expecting the worst from people.
what it means: preview the day's friction, recall a principle, set an intention, so you meet the day as yourself.

what a scholar hears: Meditations 2.1 previews difficult people but calls them kin; 3.13 keeps principles ready like a doctor's instruments; 5.1 asks whether he was made to lie warm under the blankets.

sources.quoted: Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busy-body, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial.

notes: Meditations 2.1 quoted from Long 1862: confirm exact wording and punctuation.
Meditations 3.13 (as physicians have instruments ready for sudden cases, keep your principles ready) and 5.1 (were you made to lie under the bedclothes and keep warm?) paraphrased. Confirm.
'Praemeditatio malorum' is a later Latin label (from Cicero's 'praemeditatio futurorum malorum', Tusculan Disputations 3.29); confirm phrasing.
Three-step morning is a modern synthesis of ancient practices; the script says it is gathered mostly from Marcus.
